items.title: Shapley fields reveal mosaic chemotopic organization in the mouse Olfactory bulb across diverse chemical feature sets
items.summary: by Nikola Milićević, Shawn D. Burton, Matt Wachowiak, Vladimir Itskov Neural representations in the olfactory bulb (OB) remain poorly understood compared to well-established coding principles in other sensory systems. This difficulty arises because a natural coordinate system for olfactory stimulus space has not yet been identified, complicating the characterization of neural receptive fields analogous to those in other sensory modalities. Moreover, the extent to which these tuning properties are spatially organized within the OB remains unclear. To advance our understanding of the olfactory coding, we introduce an interpretable method of Shapley fields, as an olfactory analog of retinotopic receptive fields.

items.title: Bayesian efficient coding
items.summary: by Il Memming Park, Jonathan W. Pillow The efficient coding hypothesis, which proposes that neurons are optimized to maximize information about the environment, has provided a guiding theoretical framework for sensory and systems neuroscience. More recently, a theory known as the Bayesian Brain hypothesis has focused on the brain’s ability to integrate sensory and prior sources of information in order to perform Bayesian inference. Although pieces of a connection between these two hypotheses have appeared in prior work, a general formulation that treats the optimality criterion as an arbitrary functional of the posterior distribution – and thereby admits both information-based and other objectives within a single framework – has remained largely implicit.

items.title: A heat-induced HagF-HrcA regulatory loop promotes chlamydial fitness and infectious progeny yield under stress
items.summary: by Yehong Huang, Yuxuan Wang, Matthew Pan, Danny Wan, Lingling Wang, Joseph D. Fondell, Xiang Wu, Guangming Zhong, Huizhou Fan Bacterial survival under environmental stress requires precise regulation of protein homeostasis, yet how this is achieved in organisms with streamlined genomes remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify HagF as a previously unrecognized protein that antagonizes the conserved heat-inducible transcriptional repressor HrcA in Chlamydia . Using genetic and biochemical approaches, including overexpression and CRISPRi-mediated knockdown, we show that under non-stressed conditions, HrcA represses hagF along with its five known targets, including hrcA and four chaperone genes. Upon heat stress, HagF is induced and binds HrcA, attenuating its repressor activity.

items.title: Improved Visualization of the Internal Branch of the Superior Laryngeal Nerve during Pharyngeal Endoscopic Subepithelial Dissection with Use of Red Dichromatic Imaging.
items.summary: Endoscopic subepithelial dissection is a minimally invasive treatment for superficial pharyngeal neoplastic lesions, requiring preservation of important neural structures such as the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (ibSLN). We report a case in which red dichromatic imaging (RDI) appeared to improve the visualization of a linear structure presumed to be the ibSLN compared with white-light imaging (WLI). A 57-year-old woman underwent endoscopic subepithelial dissection for a 5-mm superficial lesion on the pharyngoepiglottic fold. Both WLI and RDI revealed a whitish linear structure beneath the lesion, which was presumed to represent the ibSLN based on its anatomical location and course.

items.title: Long-term Endoscopic Evolution of a Pyloric Gland Adenoma Arising in Nonatrophic Gastric Mucosa and Initially Resembling a Fundic Gland Polyp.
items.summary: Pyloric gland adenoma (PGA) is a rare gastric epithelial neoplasm often associated with autoimmune or metaplastic atrophic gastritis. An 80-year-old man underwent serial upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. A small gastric fundus lesion initially resembling a fundic gland polyp (FGP) was followed without biopsy. Over 11 years, it enlarged to 22 mm and became increasingly whitish, against a background described endoscopically as nonatrophic. Biopsy suggested PGA, and the lesion was resected en bloc by endoscopic submucosal dissection. Closely packed pyloric-type glands showed elongation, tortuosity, branching, and cystic dilatation, with diffuse MUC6 expression and MUC5AC expression restricted to the surface epithelium. The lesion was diagnosed as PGA with low-grade dysplasia.

items.title: Enhanced Esophageal Cancer Detection Using Spectrum-Aided Vision Enhancer: A Comparative Study of White Light Imaging, Narrow-Band Imaging, and Algorithmic Narrow-Band Imaging-Like Imaging.
items.summary: Background and aims Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) detection is crucial for improving survival. While narrow-band imaging (NBI) improves mucosal visualization, limitations remain. We evaluated the diagnostic performance of the Spectrum-Aided Vision Enhancer (SAVE), an algorithmic NBI-like technology reconstructed from white light imaging (WLI). Methods We conducted a retrospective, image-based exploratory feasibility study to descriptively evaluate the diagnostic performance of WLI, NBI, and SAVE. A dataset of 1350 still endoscopic images (450 each for WLI, NBI, and SAVE) across normal mucosa, dysplasia, and ESCC stages from 158 patients was blindly reviewed by three endoscopists with different experience levels (3, 5, and 15 years).
items.author: Wu JW, Wang YK, Mukundan A, Karmakar R, Nhu NNQ, Nagisetti Y, Liao WC, Han ML, Wu IC, Wang HC.

items.title: Generating Real-World Evidence From AI Deployed in Health Systems.
items.summary: Background Health systems increasingly deploy predictive and generative artificial intelligence (AI) to improve care delivery and outcomes. Predictive AI models estimate the risk of future events to inform targeted interventions, while generative AI systems extract, summarize, and communicate information and may automate selected tasks. Routine deployment generates clinical, operational, and interaction data that can support evaluation of the effectiveness and safety of AI-enabled workflows. Methods We review approaches to generating real-world evidence (RWE) from routine deployment of predictive and generative AI across four implementation configurations: silent deployment, human-in-the-loop (HITL), human-on-the-loop (HOTL), and automated. For each configuration, we describe the evaluation questions, routinely generated data, and feasible study designs.
items.author: Poursoltan L, Boussina A, Cao J, Kim E, Bedmutha PS, Majmudar H, Ramsis M, Khalessi A, Singh K.

items.title: EFhd2 regulates microtubule-dependent mitochondrial fitness at the B cell immune synapse.
items.summary: Immobilized antigen induces an immune synapse, which is supported by Swiprosin-1/EFhd2 (EFhd2) in B and T cells. Here, we find that EFhd2 regulates mitochondrial fitness in the B cell synapse. Whereas activated EFhd2-deficient (KO) B cells show higher mitochondrial mass than wildtype (WT) B cells, this potential advantage reverses on coated anti-IgM antibodies: activated WT B cells enhance basal and maximal respiration as well as proton leak, with large increments of mitochondrial spare capacity, but EFhd2KO B cells fail to do so. Actin destabilization, but much more so microtubule destabilization, impairs mitochondrial up-regulation in WT, but not in EFhd2KO B cells.

items.title: IAP retrotransposons contribute to the transcriptional diversity of the murine placenta.
items.summary: Transposable elements (TEs) have made important contributions to the evolution of the placenta, being co-opted to form key placental genes, as well as trophoblast-specific gene regulatory elements. But although multiple TE subfamilies have been shown to act as transcriptional enhancers in early mouse trophoblast development, it remains unclear to what extent TEs regulate placental gene expression after the establishment of a functional foetal-maternal interface. Here, we characterised the TE regulatory and transcriptional landscape in mouse placenta and gauged their evolutionary dynamics. We found that the overall gene regulatory potential of TEs is greatly diminished in differentiated mouse trophoblasts when compared to their stem cell counterpart.

items.title: Diacylglycerol kinase kappa is a target of the Prader-Willi syndrome gene SNORD116 .
items.summary: SNORD116 is a small nucleolar RNA deficient in Prader-Willi syndrome individuals. The mechanisms by which SNORD116 conveys its effects are unknown. Here, transcriptomic analysis showed that diacylglycerol kinase kappa ( Dgkk ) expression was elevated in the hypothalamus of Snord116 -deficient mice. In silico analyses predicted a strong RNA:RNA interaction between Snord116 and Dgkk mRNA that is fully conserved in mouse and human. In vitro experiments in human cellular models demonstrated that SNORD116 mediates 2'-O-methylation of DGKK mRNA and regulates DGKK mRNA and protein expression. In Snord116 -deficient mouse neurons, increased Dgkk expression was associated with attenuated diacylglycerol-mediated activation of ERK and PKC, critical elements in neuronal signaling cascades.
items.author: Zhang Y, Guo K, Batzli GF, Zhao H, Burnett LC, LeDuc CA, Stratigopoulos G, Carolan DG, Doege CA, Shen Y, Leibel RL.

items.title: Sickle Cell Trait and Incident Ischemic Stroke Risk: A Whole-Genome Sequencing Study in the All of Us Research Program.
items.summary: Background and objectives Sickle cell trait (SCT), the heterozygous hemoglobin variant (HbAS) genotype, affects approximately 300 million individuals worldwide and 8-10% of Black/African American individuals in the United States. Previous studies examining the association between SCT and ischemic stroke have yielded conflicting results, with effect estimates ranging from null to more than 2-fold increased risk. Interpretation of this literature has been limited by modest sample sizes, restricted ancestral diversity, and incomplete adjustment for genetic ancestry. We therefore evaluated whether whole-genome sequencing (WGS) confirmed SCT was independently associated with incident ischemic stroke after adjustment for genetic ancestry and vascular risk factors in the All of Us (AoU) cohort.

items.title: Correlating Laryngoscopic and Clinical Findings With Airway Intervention in Angioedema.
items.summary: Objectives To evaluate whether specific presenting symptoms and laryngoscopic subsite involvement in aerodigestive angioedema predict clinical severity, defined by airway intervention, hospital admission, and length of stay (LOS). A secondary objective was to assess the performance of a reduced symptom-based model for predicting intubation. Methods A retrospective cohort study was performed of adult patients presenting with aerodigestive angioedema at a single tertiary academic medical center between January 2013 and January 2023. Data were abstracted from electronic medical records. Presenting symptoms and laryngoscopic subsites of edema were recorded. The primary outcome was airway intervention. Secondary outcomes included hospital admission and LOS.

items.title: Tailor-Made Hybrid Pulsed-Field and Radiofrequency Ablation Guided by ExTRa Mapping for Refractory Long-Standing Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: First Experience With the Affera System Prism-2.
items.summary: Background Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) alone is frequently insufficient for persistent atrial fibrillation (AF). Although pulsed-field ablation (PFA) ensures durable linear lesions, extensive transmural ablation risks iatrogenic atrial tachycardia. A tailored strategy combining PFA with titrated radiofrequency (RF) energy for mild substrate homogenization remains poorly defined. Case summary A 77-year-old male with post-stroke refractory long-standing AF underwent a re-do ablation. Biatrial substrate evaluation was performed using the ExTRa mapping system, enabled by the Affera system (Prism-2) to visualize the nonmagnetic 20-pole spiral catheter. Areas with a mean non-passively activated ratio (%NP) ≥ 35% and low voltage ( Conclusion The hybrid PFA/RF system integrated with AI-driven phase mapping enables a safe, non-destructive, tailor-made substrate modification strategy for refractory persistent AF.

items.title: Dynamic force-induced nucleoporin stretch mechanomemory prolongs nuclear pore complex dilation and importin transport.
items.summary: How the nuclear pore complex (NPC) is dynamically regulated by mechanical stimuli is poorly understood. Herein, using FRET (fluorescence resonance energy transfer) spectroscopy and MINFLUX (MINimal fluorescence photon FLUXes) nanoscopy, we demonstrate that external local mechanical and global osmotic stresses to the surface of mammalian cells induced mechanomemory of nucleoporin (NUP) deformation. During and long after (∼30 min) local stress application via integrins or global hypo-osmotic stress, the FRET ratio of YFP-NUP62 (acceptor) to CFP-NUP88 (donor) decreased and remained low, suggesting that the distance between the two NUPs increased and the NUPs were stretched. Independent MINFLUX measurements of NPC strain memory following the same local mechanical or global osmotic stress mirrored the magnitude of NUP strain memory in the NPC observed via FRET.

items.title: Optimizing Cochlear Implant Programming in Single-Sided Deafness and Asymmetric Hearing Loss: A Randomized Comparison of ESRT and Behavioral Methods.
items.summary: Objectives To compare outcomes of electrically evoked stapedial reflex threshold (ESRT) and behavioral programming methods in cochlear implant (CI) recipients with single-sided deafness (SSD) and asymmetric hearing loss (AHL). Methods Ten participants (mean age 43.9 years; 60% female; 60% non-Hispanic) with SSD (90%) or AHL (10%) were enrolled in a prospective randomized crossover study. Participants with SSD/AHL and at least 3 months of CI experience were programmed with ipsilateral ESRT (Ipsi ESRT), contralateral ESRT (Contra ESRT), and behavioral methods (Behav MCL) in randomized order. Outcome measures included speech perception (CNC words, BKB-SIN sentences), daily CI device use, and hearing-related CI quality of life (SSQ-12).

items.title: Strengthening antimicrobial stewardship through an international multicentre improvement programme of hospitals serving deprived populations.
items.summary: Background Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) is essential to addressing antimicrobial resistance, but its implementation remains variable, particularly in settings with resource limitations. Hospitals serving deprived or underserved populations often work with limited diagnostic capacity, workforce pressures and variable digital infrastructure, which shape stewardship delivery. The Antimicrobial Stewardship Disparities Programme (ASDP) was established to strengthen stewardship capability in such settings and to support progress towards accreditation under the Global AMS Accreditation Scheme (GAMSAS). Methods A mixed-methods evaluation was undertaken across six centres in Botswana, Kenya, Lebanon, Mexico, Pakistan and the USA. Centres completed baseline and end of programme self-assessments against 17 AMS, infection prevention and control (IPC) and laboratory standards mapped to 4 pillars (structures, guidance, education and surveillance).

items.title: Identifying pregnant women with severe fear of childbirth using the Japanese version of the Wijma Delivery Expectancy/Experience Questionnaire: A cross-sectional study.
items.summary: Aim This study aimed to investigate, separately among primiparas and multiparas, whether qualitatively distinct groups based on fear of childbirth (FOC) could be identified using the Japanese version of the Wijma Delivery Expectancy/Experience Questionnaire (JW-DEQ), and to identify groups characterized by severe FOC. It also aimed to determine JW-DEQ cut-off scores for severe FOC and associated factors. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted between May 2019 and January 2020. Pregnant women at ≥35 weeks of gestation were recruited from 26 obstetric facilities in Japan. Two-step cluster analysis was performed using four JW-DEQ subscales. Multiple logistic regression identified factors associated with severe FOC.

items.title: Biodiversity and Food Security in Sub-Saharan Africa: Evidence From a Dynamic Spatial Durbin Model.
items.summary: This study examines the effect of biodiversity on food security in 40 Sub-Saharan African countries over the period 2001-2022. Food security is measured using a composite Food Security Index constructed through Principal Component Analysis, while biodiversity is proxied by the Red List Index. To account for temporal persistence, spatial dependence and cross-country spillover effects, the analysis employs a Dynamic Spatial Durbin Model. The results indicate that biodiversity has no statistically significant effect on the aggregate Food Security Index in either the short or the long run. However, disaggregated analyses reveal that biodiversity significantly improves Average Dietary Energy Supply Adequacy and the Share of Dietary Energy Supply Derived from Cereals, Roots and Tubers but has no significant effect on Average Protein Supply or Per Capita Food Supply Variability.

items.title: Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic strategies to optimize antifungal therapy, prevent resistance and minimize treatment failure.
items.summary: Invasive fungal diseases (IFDs) present significant challenges in clinical practice due to high morbidity and mortality rates, compounded by antifungal resistance, diagnostic limitations and pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) complexities. The main antifungal classes, triazoles, polyenes, echinocandins and pyrimidine analogues, are essential for managing IFDs but are increasingly undermined by resistance due to genetic mutations, efflux pump over-expression and biofilm formation. Some fungal pathogens, such as Candidozyma auris , can resist multiple antifungal classes by deploying a combination of mechanisms. PK/PD indices, including C max /minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), AUC/MIC and percentage of time (% T ) > MIC, are essential for optimizing antifungal therapy and improving the likelihood of adequate efficacy, while potentially limiting resistance selection through improved exposure.

items.title: Methodological and Theoretical Advances in Research on Grooming in Child Sexual Abuse.
items.summary: The science of the dynamics, consequences and treatment of child sexual abuse developed rapidly after passage of the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act of 1974. However, the necessity for some set of methods to both evaluate and treat the unexpected number of survivors of child abuse led to both innovation and controversy. One contribution that has deepened our understanding of child abuse is the enhanced attention to the grooming process, a term first offered to the field by Jon Conte in 1984. Virtually all experts agree that knowledge and accurate identification of this process as it is occurring would aid prevention.

items.summary: This brief opinion outlines the increase in homicide of women by intimate partners, primarily with guns. I make the case that more than half of abused women want to stay with their abusive intimate partners for many complex reasons and that they want to stay safely. They are not being controlled by abusers but rather making rational decisions based on their observations of, and love for the abuser, and concerns for their children. In order for women to stay safely, we need to get more of the abusers into interventions that have been shown to be effective, like Strength At Home and also store guns safely.

items.title: Auditing Biomedical Literature with Blinded AI Peer Review: Where Peer Review Works, Where It Fails, and How to Strengthen It
items.summary: Biomedical publishing has grown more than elevenfold since 1991, outstripping human peer review. Unblinded language models cannot audit this literature objectively because they recognize famous authors and journals from training memory. We built BARS (Blinded AI Review System), an automated referee that strips titles, author names, institutions, journal headers, and dates before grading full-text manuscripts on a 10-point scale covering methods, evidence, biology, and reproducibility. We used BARS to generate 1,874 blind reviews across 1,714 unique papers. BARS passed 100% of verified sound controls, caught 77% to 91% of internally flawed papers, eliminated a +0.35-point prestige boost, and more than doubled human referee consistency.
items.author: Kosakovsky Pond, S. L., Pond, S. J. K., Weaver, S. et al.

items.title: Conserved synaptic modifications by humanized tau through diverse isoform- and mutation-specific intracellular interactions
items.summary: Mutations in the microtubule-binding protein tau are considered causal for a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively referred to as primary tauopathies. Specific tauopathies are associated with different mutations, distinct tau isoforms, manifest in unique cellular and circuit-wide patterns of degeneration, and present with specific clinical symptoms and trajectories. The mechanisms that link variations in the primary tau protein structure to distinct forms of neural circuit dysfunction remain largely unknown. Here, we created an orthogonal viral resource to systematically examine the impact of expressing humanized tau isoforms harboring different disease-relevant mutations in excitatory pyramidal cells from the mouse prelimbic cortex.
items.author: Nickerson, E., Pomeroy-Tuck, J., Pratt, S. et al.

items.title: Serial dependence carries the action that produced the previous report
items.summary: Serial dependence pulls current judgments toward the recent past, but what is carried forward is debated: the previous stimulus, the previous decision, or something about the report itself. Three magnitude-reproduction experiments separated these sources. Participants viewed dot arrays that varied independently in duration and numerosity, then reproduced the cued dimension by holding a key while a display accumulated, so that both magnitudes were produced through the same action. A response-history model partitioned the attraction into previous-stimulus and previous-response paths. The previous response predicted cross-dimensional attraction after controlling for the previous and current stimuli: a numerosity report biased the next duration judgment and vice versa (Experiment 1), also when each task used its own response key (Experiment 2).
items.author: Qu, C., Naeve, C., Shi, Z.

items.title: Mitochondria-Coupled Hitchhiking Drives Vimentin Intermediate Filament Transport
items.summary: Vimentin intermediate filaments (VIFs) undergo active microtubule-dependent transport throughout the cell, with trajectories resembling those of motor-driven organelles, yet our recent work showed that only a small subset of VIFs lies close to microtubules. How VIFs engage the microtubule-based transport machinery, and whether additional transport routes contribute, remain unresolved. We hypothesized that VIFs move indirectly, by hitchhiking on motile organelles, and tested this using mitochondria. Live imaging showed mitochondria and adjacent VIFs moving together, and volume electron microscopy revealed VIFs closely following mitochondrial surfaces at sites distinct from microtubule contacts. Depleting the mitochondrial motor adaptor TRAK1 to inhibit anterograde mitochondrial transport shifted both mitochondria and VIFs toward the nucleus.
items.author: Renganathan, B., Moore, A. S., Adam, S. A. et al.

items.title: Sex-specific bone marrow populations regulate skeletal phenotype and identify CD74-marked osteoclast precursor subsets
items.summary: While there are clear differences in bone accrual and maintenance between men and women due to hormonal regulation, the potential cell-intrinsic factors governing this difference are poorly understood. To investigate this, we performed bone marrow transplantation assays using male or female bone marrow transplantation into male hosts. Micro-CT analyses of lethally irradiated 8-week-old male mice transplanted with female bone marrow exhibited increased vertebral body trabecular and cortical bone mass. To identify cell types mediating these effects, we performed comparative single cell sequencing analyses and identified several CD11B+CD74+ myeloid cell clusters. Male donor BM chimeric mice had a higher proportion of Cd74-expressing clusters compared to female donor BM chimeric mice.
items.author: Koroth, J., Karkache, I. Y., Vu, E. K. et al.

items.title: PPI-Rescue: restoration of eye development via functional reconstitution of a transcription complex.
items.summary: The activity of transcription factors (TFs) can be modulated through protein-protein interactions (PPIs) with cofactors which can serve to enhance, repress or alter the specificity of TF function. Current genetic and molecular approaches such as knockout and overexpression studies are likely to affect all possible activities of a TF, presenting a dilemma when attempting to parse out how TFs function within a cell. Hence, there is a need to devise a technique that will allow for mechanistic insight to be gained into the function(s) of discrete transcription complexes. Herein we report ''PPI-Rescue'', an approach that leverages bespoke mutations in TFs and the selective reconstitution of specific complexes to study the molecular properties and biological functions of discrete transcription complexes in vitro and in vivo.
items.author: Jusic, N., Pina, C., Netz, D. et al.

items.title: Habitat degradation destabilizes complex metacommunities by disrupting dispersal
items.summary: Habitat loss and fragmentation are rapidly reshaping ecosystems worldwide, yet their consequences for ecological stability remain unresolved. Classical theory, pioneered by Robert May, established rigorous criteria for stability; however, these apply to spatially well-mixed communities, limiting their relevance to habitat degradation. Here, we develop a metacommunity framework that integrates classical stability theory with spatial dynamics to determine how anthropogenic habitat degradation reshapes ecosystem stability. We show that metacommunities exhibit three distinct dynamical regimes following a perturbation (e.g., drought or forest fire): stable regime (perturbations decay and species persist), reactive regime (perturbations are transiently amplified, which increases extinction risk under repeated disturbances), and unstable regime (perturbations grow, causing extinctions even after a single disturbance).
items.author: Sun, Y., Yin, X., Jin, Z. et al.

items.title: Protein language models learn the underlying accessibility of mutations alongside protein fitness landscapes
items.summary: Protein language models (PLMs) score the effects of amino acid replacements as pseudo-probabilities, which are widely utilised to map protein fitness landscapes. However, because their training data relies on natural amino acid sequences, these models conflate protein structural constraints with nucleotide mutation biases and codon accessibility. Using the rapid emergence of the divergent influenza A H3N2 K lineage as a stress test, we investigate how base PLMs (ESM-2 and ESM-C) versus fine-tuned versions of these models capture mutational processes. We systematically implement a parameter sweep to explicitly couple (or decouple) empirical nucleotide mutational supply from PLM-assessed amino acid substitution pseudo-probabilities across evolutionary forecasting tasks.
items.author: MacLean, O. A., Lamb, K., Lytras, S. et al.

items.title: Novel Regulators of Sugar-dependent Food Consumption in Drosophila melanogaster
items.summary: Diet and genetic background interact to influence food consumption, yet the genetic basis of diet-dependent feeding behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we used genome-wide association analysis (GWAS) to investigate the genetic regulation of sugar-dependent food consumption in Drosophila melanogaster. Food intake was quantified in 176 lines of the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) using the Con-Ex (Consumption-Excretion) assay on low- and high-sugar foods. Flies showed compensatory feeding, consuming more low-sugar food than high-sugar food, and this behavior was largely maintained across genotypes. Additionally, the magnitude and overall consumption varied several-fold among lines, with broad-sense heritability of 0.53 to 0.66 across sexes and diets.
items.author: Opoola, M. A., Fitzgerald, L., Ahmed, S. et al.

items.title: Actin pool controls the scaling of dynamic actin networks
items.summary: Scaling is a fundamental property of living systems, allowing cells to match the size of their internal components to their volume. The size and shape of cells depend largely on the actin cytoskeleton, whose dynamic self-assembling structures are central to this adaptation. Yet how they self-assemble in a volume-dependent manner remains unresolved. To address this question, we used a biomimetic system consisting of beads propelled by actin polymerization in microwells of different volumes, which allowed us to work with a limited and defined number of components. This approach enabled the first reconstitution, from purified proteins, of dynamic cytoskeletal structures that adapt to the volume of their environment.
items.author: Cantat, A., Guerin, C., Morel, N. et al.

items.title: Structural basis of ribosomal RNA repair by RtcB2
items.summary: Ribotoxins disable ribosomes by cleaving ribosomal RNA, but how repair enzymes recognize and restore these damaged machines remains unclear. Here, we report three cryo-electron microscopy structures of the RNA ligase RtcB2 bound to damaged Escherichia coli 30S subunits. An extended interface stabilizes the ribosomal head and decoding-center scaffold while positioning the cleaved 3'-phosphate end within the catalytic pocket. Two structures contain enzyme-linked guanosine monophosphate, whereas the third captures its transfer to the RNA. RNA activation accompanies RtcB2 reorientation and entry of the 5'-hydroxyl-containing segment into an adjacent cleft. Comparisons with assembled ribosomes reveal structural barriers to substrate access. These structures connect recognition of a damaged ribosome to chemical activation of its RNA for repair.
items.author: Tian, Y., Zhou, Q., Yu, Q. et al.

items.title: Bicarbonate-free pH neutralization resensitizes ovarian cancer to chemotherapy and is tracked by 3T CEST MRI
items.summary: Ovarian tumors that initially respond to platinum-taxane chemotherapy often relapse as chemoresistant disease. The acidic tumor microenvironment is a well-known but under-exploited driver of this resistance, and neutralization strategies such as oral bicarbonate have not translated. Here we show that inhibiting specific tumor pH regulators at noncytotoxic doses relieves acidosis and restores frontline chemotherapy, monitored noninvasively at clinical 3T. In OVCAR3 and SKOV-3 ovarian cancer cells, MCT1 and MCT4 were overexpressed under acidosis, and the MCT4 inhibitor acriflavine reduced extracellular acidification at concentrations well below its cytotoxic IC50, without bicarbonate buffering. Acidosis blunted the efficacy of both paclitaxel and carboplatin, raising their IC50 values, which acriflavine reversed.
items.author: Patkulkar, P. A., Mandal, A., Noble, S. et al.

items.title: Transferrin receptor binding valency determines the circulating half-life and weight-loss efficacy of Fc-FGF21 in TfR-humanized mice
items.summary: Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) is a promising metabolic hormone with potent anti-obesity effects. It acts in both the central nervous system and peripheral tissues to exert its metabolic benefits. Because its receptors are expressed at low levels in the brain, we hypothesized that enhanced transport across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) would improve its efficacy. To achieve this, FGF21 was fused to Fc(TV35), an engineered Fc fragment that binds the human transferrin receptor (hTfR), to generate Fc(TV35)-FGF21. Fc(TV35)-FGF21 does not bind to mouse TfR, so it produced weight-loss effects in wild-type diet-induced obese mice comparable to those of Fc-FGF21. However, it failed to induce weight loss in homozygous hTfR-humanized mice because of a markedly shortened circulating half-life.
items.author: Zhou, H., Deng, Y., Li, H. et al.

items.title: Live Droplet Single-Cell RNA Sequencing
items.summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing has emerged as one of the most influential methods of the past decade, enabling the dissection of cellular heterogeneity and the discovery of rare cell types. However, most workflows require cell lysis and provide only terminal snapshots, limiting their ability to capture dynamic cellular trajectories and temporal variations within the same cell. Herein, we present Live Droplet single-cell RNA sequencing (Live D-seq), a technology that enables scalable transcriptome-wide profiling of individual living cells over time. Live D-seq combines longitudinal intracellular sampling of live, barcoded cells with particle-templated emulsification and barcoded hydrogel beads, enabling repeated samples from the same cell lineage to be linked across time points.
items.author: Reynolds, D. E., Lee, S., Oh, D. et al.

items.title: Adaptation of breast cancer cells to serum-free defined medium reveals changes in proliferation, adhesion, and lipid metabolism
items.summary: Cancer cell metabolic dependencies are strongly influenced by nutrient availability, yet conventional culture conditions contain non-physiological nutrient concentrations and poorly defined serum components that may obscure metabolic vulnerabilities. Here, we investigated the adaptation of three breast cancer cell lines to physiologically relevant, serum-free defined medium (DM). Using a stepwise reduction in fetal bovine serum (FBS), we evaluated proliferation, adhesion, morphology, and transcriptional changes in HER2-positive SK-BR-3, triple-negative MDA-MB-231, and ER-positive/HER2-positive BT-474 cells. The three cell lines differed substantially in their ability to adapt to serum-free conditions. MDA-MB-231 cells adapted readily, maintaining proliferation and adhesion without exogenous substrate coatings. SK-BR-3 cells also achieved sustained proliferation in serum-free DM, but required a serum-derived coating to maintain adhesion.
items.author: Aarrestad, C., Khatib, T. O., Alvarez, J. V.

items.title: Lineage tracing in rhabdoid tumor organoids and orthotopic xenografts reveals convergent transcriptional states
items.summary: Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are aggressive pediatric malignancies driven by loss of a single SWI/SNF subunit in an otherwise near-silent genome, yet they display extensive transcriptional heterogeneity. Whether this heterogeneity reflects the outgrowth of transcriptionally distinct clones, or states adopted independently of lineage, is unknown. Here we combined lentiviral lineage barcoding with single-cell RNA sequencing in two patient-derived renal MRT organoid models, followed through long-term in vitro culture and in a novel orthotopic xenograft setting. In both modalities, tumors and cultures became progressively restricted to a small number of lineages, and the clones that expanded were transcriptionally distinct from one another.
items.author: Perticari, G., DeMartino, J., Fumagalli, A. et al.

items.title: Histopathological and virus-associated features of Boid Inclusion Body Disease in Boa constrictor
items.summary: Boid inclusion body disease (BIBD) is a reptarenavirus-induced fatal disease of boid snakes that, while diagnosed with ease due to the pathognomonic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (IB), is not yet fully characterized pathomorphologically and with regards to its pathogenesis. The present study retrospectively investigated a random cohort of 50 captive male and female boa constrictors of variable age (neonate to 25 years) for histopathological changes and in situ viral protein (nucleoprotein, NP, and glycoprotein 2, GP2) expression patterns. IB formation and NP expression were scored semiquantitatively. The vast majority of snakes (42/50; 84%) exhibited histopathological changes; these mainly (39/42; 93%) represented inflammatory processes that most frequently affected the gastrointestinal tract.
items.author: Bogner, M., Dervas, E., De Neck, S. et al.

items.title: Vorinostat Can Reduce an Ongoing Fibrosis and Preserve Key Liver Metabolic Functions by Selectively Altering Mesenchymal Cell Differentiation
items.summary: Liver fibrosis is a major global cause of mortality that is driven by the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) into extracellular matrix (ECM)-producing myofibroblasts (MyoFs). The lack of predictive human in vitro models has severely hampered the discovery of targeted anti-fibrotic therapies. Here, we describe a human iPSC-derived hepatic micro-organoid (microHO) model, which labels collagen producing cells, to study liver fibrosis pathophysiology and screen drug candidates. We discovered that while multiple drugs prevented fibrosis when co-administered prophylactically with TGF{beta}1, only the FDA-approved pan-HDAC inhibitor Vorinostat (SAHA) successfully reduced an established, ongoing fibrosis and preserved life-sustaining liver metabolic functions in a fibrotic microenvironment, including ammonia detoxification and CYP3A4-mediated drug metabolism.
items.author: GUAN, Y., Peltz, G.

items.title: Site-, strain- and mutation-specific osteopetrosis phenotypes in mice with Clcn7 variants
items.summary: Background: Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II (ADOII) is a rare bone disorder caused primarily by heterozygous mutations in CLCN7 and characterized by increased bone mass yet fragility and marked phenotypic heterogeneity among affected individuals. The biological factors underlying this variability remain poorly understood. We investigated the effects of age, sex, genetic background, and mutation type on bone phenotypes in murine models of ADOII carrying heterozygous Clcn7 F318L/+ or G213R/+ mutations. Methods: Bone microarchitecture was assessed by micro-computed tomography in vertebrae and femora from female and male mice across multiple ages (12, 24, and 52 weeks) and strain backgrounds (FVB/NJ, C57BL/6, and 129).
items.author: Shimonty, A., Dahl, X. G., Zboinski, E. et al.

items.title: The chloroplast-localised transporter RETICULATA controls palisade mesophyll cell division and expansion
items.summary: Plant leaves contain extensive intercellular air spaces, which contribute to photosynthetic capacity and water use efficiency in different environments. Despite this importance, the developmental mechanisms that control leaf air space patterning are poorly understood. For over 20 years it has been known that plants with disrupted chloroplast biogenesis and metabolism have increased intercellular air spaces, but the underlying molecular mechanism is unknown. Here, we characterise leaf air space morphogenesis in mutants of the chloroplast amino acid transporter RETICULATA (RE), which has enlarged air spaces. We show that the reticulata-6 (re-6) loss of function mutant exhibits increased air space expansion specifically in the palisade, and not the spongy, mesophyll.
items.author: Locke Bevia, E. A., Aldorino, E., Fitzsimons, J. M. et al.

items.title: Anionic lipids stabilize etioplast prolamellar bodies and facilitate thylakoid biogenesis during etioplast-to-chloroplast differentiation
items.summary: Etioplasts of dark-grown angiosperm seedlings contain prolamellar bodies (PLBs), lattice-like membranes that are quickly transformed into thylakoids upon illumination. Phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol (SQDG) are major anionic lipids in these membranes, but their roles in etioplast-to-chloroplast differentiation remain unclear. We analyzed Arabidopsis thaliana mutants with reduced PG biosynthesis (pgp1-1), complete SQDG deficiency (sqd1), and the pgp1-1 sqd1 double mutant. Although pgp1-1 etioplasts showed a loosened PLB lattice when fixed under white light, they retained regular, wild-type-like lattices when fixed under infrared light, suggesting that their PLBs were more susceptible to light-induced disassembly. The rapid PLB disassembly in pgp1-1 upon illumination was accompanied by rapid conversion of dark-accumulated protochlorophyllide to chlorophyll and lamellar membrane formation, suggesting a link between membrane remodeling and chlorophyll formation.
items.author: Yoshihara, A., Uwatoko, R., Kobayashi, K. et al.

items.title: Consequence and further analysis of the minor role of daylength in the floral initiation of sorghum crops
items.summary: Background and Aims Flowering time is assumed to be primarily controlled by daylength, but field observations disagree. For instance, mid-early sorghum varieties sown at the same time at tropical and temperate latitudes have similar flowering dates. We previously proposed an alternative framework integrating daily changes in sunrise and sunset times (dSR and dSS). Methods Variety trials of mid-late varieties from the Northern Hemisphere were carried out in Madagascar and in Argentina. Series of monthly sowings of 28 varieties were carried out in Mali between 2000 and 2009. Heading date and, in Mali, panicle initiation (PI) were recorded. Key Results In Madagascar and in Argentina mid-late varieties headed late or very late when sown in November and December, consistent with the higher dSR/dSS values of the southern hemisphere summer.
items.author: Clerget, B., Sidibe, M., vom Brocke, K. et al.

items.title: Nociceptive-evoked electroencephalography can predict inter-individual differences in high frequency induced sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
items.summary: Evoked-EEG can capture changes in cortical responses during experimentally induced sensitised pain states. However, the test-retest reliability of such methods requires validation. The present study applied HFS across two identical sessions in the same individuals to assess the test-retest reliability of EEG dynamics evoked by a 128mN pin-prick stimulator and single-pulse electrical stimuli before and after HFS conditioning. The value of these features for reflecting individual differences in the development of hyperalgesia was also assessed. Results demonstrate poor-to-moderate test-retest reliability and relatively wide agreement at baseline for all features, with lateralised differences often present. This was further reduced when post-HFS changes were considered.
items.author: Mugglestone, S., Hughes, S. W., Ganis, G.

items.title: Automated Segmentation of the Hypothalamus: Associations of Age and Socioeconomic Status with Subunit Volumes in Cognitively Healthy Adults
items.summary: Background: The hypothalamus regulates sleep-wake cycles, energy balance, and autonomic and neuroendocrine function, yet its small size and poorly contrasted boundaries have long hindered in vivo volumetry. Deep-learning segmentation now allows the hypothalamus to be divided into functionally meaningful subunits. We examined whether hypothalamic subunit volumes are associated with age and socioeconomic status (SES) in cognitively healthy adults. Methods: From the OASIS-1 cross-sectional dataset (n = 416, 18-96 years), 133 participants with a Clinical Dementia Rating of 0 and complete segmentation output were analysed (33-94 years). A FreeSurfer-based convolutional neural network, run on a cloud virtual machine, segmented five subunits per hemisphere.
items.author: Akar, B., Atasever, U.

items.title: Gain Control of Peripheral Input by Core Brain Thermosensors Drives Drosophila Thermoregulation
items.summary: Temperature affects all aspects of animal physiology, rendering thermoregulation critical for survival. In Drosophila larvae, well-established peripheral thermosensors detect temperature changes and mediate thermotaxis over a broad innocuous range, but how larvae seek a specific preferred body temperature within this range remains unknown. Here we show that core thermosensors in the brain (LPBT neurons) establish this setpoint by mediating warming-evoked turning at temperatures above it. LPBTs express the warmth-activated thermosensor TrpA1(A), but are not simply cell-autonomous thermosensors. Rather, sustained LPBT responses above setpoint require both peripheral thermosensory input and TRPA1-dependent thermosensing within LPBTs. TRPA1-dependent core thermosensing provides gain control that defines the homeostatic setpoint by tuning the behavioral weights of peripheral inputs.
items.author: Lazopulo, S., Zlatic, M., Cardona, A. et al.

items.title: Brain Decoding from a Deep Neural Network of Visual Memory Reveals the Maturation Trajectory of Memory Systems across Ages 3-7
items.summary: Memories from the first four years of life are largely inaccessible by adulthood, yet these early experiences profoundly shape cognition throughout development. Understanding this phenomenon of infantile amnesia is critical for revealing the mechanisms of early memory development. Here, we developed a new content-based behavioral measure of memory that quantifies how closely children's memory patterns resemble those of adults, which we term the memory maturation score. Using a movie-watching fMRI dataset spanning age 3 to adulthood, we trained a cross-validated model on adults' movie-evoked brain activity to predict adult's propensity to remember each movie snippet, estimated by ResMem, a deep neural network trained to predict visual memorability.
items.author: GUO, X., Leong, Y. C., Bainbridge, W. A.

items.title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity
items.summary: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives.
items.author: Minasi, C. B., Hassan, U., Cline, C. C. et al.

items.title: Rapid Detection and Initial Treatment of Life-Threatening Subdural Hematoma in a Sheep Model
items.summary: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in people under 40 worldwide. There is an unmet need for detection and treatment of life-threatening TBI when computed tomography (CT) scanners and neurosurgeons are unavailable. We developed a new handheld frequency-domain multidetector infrared hemorrhage detection device. Using the new device, military pre-hospital medics required <4 minutes to detect life-threatening subdural hematoma in a sheep model. We developed a second device that allows non-neurosurgeons to safely create a burr hole and partially remove clotted subdural blood. In sheep, the treatment device reduced intracranial pressure within 20 minutes, and improved post-anesthesia blinded neurological outcomes.
items.author: Brody, D. L., Dengler, B. A., Angelo, J. P. et al.

items.title: Intra-individual changes to peak alpha frequency map to pain perception following high frequency sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
items.summary: Resting-state EEG can capture cortical dynamics relevant to sensitised pain states in the absence of ongoing nociceptive engagement. However, whilst the slowing of global oscillations is evident within various chronic pain conditions, the mechanistic specificity of PAF and -band power remains uncertain. Therefore, the present study assessed these features across two identical test-retest sessions in which HFS was applied to induce the development of SHA as characterised through 128 mN MPS. Crucially, changes in -band features post-HFS were investigated. Blind source separation was also applied to identify independent sensorimotor components relevant to nociception and assess their test-retest reliability. Results demonstrated good test-retest reliability for sensor-level data at baseline, with inter-individual changes in global PAF reflecting MPS post-HFS.
items.author: Mugglestone, S., Hughes, S. W., Ganis, G.

items.title: Matching Corticospinal and Cortical Excitability along the motor cortex: TMS-EMG-EEG study
items.summary: There is still no consensus on how to choose intensities for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The resting motor threshold (RMT), the intensity needed to evoke muscle contractions in the contralateral limb muscles, is a robust muscle-specific index of corticospinal excitability. RMT from one of the hand muscles is commonly used as a reference for TMS neuromodulation interventions and TMS-electroencephalography (EEG) studies. However, it only provides an indirect measure of cortical excitability, and even for the primary motor cortex (M1), we do not understand how cortical and corticospinal excitability correspond to each other. Indeed, it remains unclear whether cortical responses to TMS follow similar location-dependent patterns along the M1, and whether subthreshold stimulation can reliably engage cortical circuits relevant to motor output.

items.title: A split nozzle and two-protein chain-like fibers define the tail architecture of Pseudomonas aeruginosa podophage A1002
items.summary: by Hao Pang, Yuan Chen, Zeng Peng, Hao Xiao, Wenyuan Chen, Xiaowu Li, Ping Chen, Jing Zheng, Hongrong Liu Phage therapy offers unique advantages against antibiotic-resistant bacteria. However, high-resolution structural studies of phages targeting Pseudomonas aeruginosa —a top-seven global pathogen—particularly podophages, remain severely limited, directly impeding structure-based development of novel antimicrobials. In this study, we utilize cryo-EM to resolve the high-resolution intact structure of mature phage A1002, a podophage infecting carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa . Based on density maps combined with AlphaFold3 predictions, we identified 11 structural protein components from the head to the tail. Phage A1002 exhibits a distinctly elongated tail morphology distinct from other reported podophages.
items.author: Hao Pang, Yuan Chen, Zeng Peng et al.

items.title: An open-source eye-tracking system adaptable to diverse terrestrial vertebrates reveals state-dependent visual acquisition in lizards
items.summary: by Nimrod Leberstein, Tali Remenick, Milan Becker, Mark Shein-Idelson Gaze shifts are fundamental to visual exploration and processing, yet empirical knowledge is largely confined to a small number of model species, limiting our understanding of general principles of visual acquisition across animals. Here, we introduce a versatile, low-cost, and open-source framework design for eye-tracking in small, freely moving animals. Leveraging photogrammetry, 3D modeling, and 3D-printing, we produce headmounts adaptable to diverse head-eye geometries, as we demonstrate for lizards, turtles, and mice. Detailed recordings in Pogona vitticeps, a laterally eyed ectotherm with a high-acuity retina, reveal a rich oculomotor repertoire with kinematics closely resembling the saccadic main sequence in primates.
items.author: Nimrod Leberstein, Tali Remenick, Milan Becker et al.

items.title: The human hippocampus supports auditory coding and multisensory integration
items.summary: by Omri Raccah, Aryan Agarwal, Yannan Zhu, Nicholas B. Turk-Browne The hippocampus receives convergent input from multiple sensory systems, yet in humans it has been studied almost exclusively through vision. Here we examine how the hippocampus contributes to sensory processing beyond the visual modality and to the multisensory integration of visual information with these other modalities. Participants were exposed to multiple repetitions of short naturalistic movie clips, each presented in four formats: auditory-only, visual-only, congruent audiovisual, and incongruent audiovisual (audio and video from different movies). Using high-resolution fMRI, we measured univariate activation and multivariate representations across the longitudinal axis and subfields of the human hippocampus.
items.author: Omri Raccah, Aryan Agarwal, Yannan Zhu et al.

items.title: A deep genetic structure phylogenomically frames the closest algal relatives of land plants
items.summary: by Maaike J. Bierenbroodspot, Cäcilia F. Kunz, Elisa S. Goldbecker, Maike Lorenz, Iker Irisarri, Thomas Pröschold, Tatyana Darienko, Jan de Vries Discerning the nature of the last common ancestor of land plants (embryophytes) and algae allows to retrace the adaptations that ushered in the conquest of land by plants. For this, the closest streptophyte algal relatives of embryophytes hold key information. Albeit initially coming as a surprise due to their plain body plans, all major phylogenomic efforts have concluded that the Zygnematophyceae are the algal sisters to land plants. The Zygnematophyceae are the streptophyte algal class with the greatest species richness and while we now have ample genome information on a few select members of zygnematophytes, our understanding of the genomic divergence as well as genetic potential for key traits is limited by a lack of phylodiverse data that accounts for this diversity and integrates it into a phylogenomic framework.
items.author: Maaike J. Bierenbroodspot, Cäcilia F. Kunz, Elisa S. Goldbecker et al.

items.title: Infant presence and mother-infant conflict predict fetal loss in wild mandrills
items.summary: by Nikolaos Smit, Berta Roura-Torres, Axelle Delaunay, Alice Baniel, Elise Huchard, Marie J. E. Charpentier Female fitness depends on reproductive pace and offspring survival, both of which are determined by the ability to balance resource allocation between current and future reproduction. Using 11 years of data on 356 pregnancies (52 of which resulted in fetal loss) from 117 wild female mandrills, we show that females who conceive while still caring for a young infant experience a greater probability of fetal loss as well as increased mother-infant behavioral conflict in the form of maternal rejection. In addition, females whose infants throw more tantrums show a greater probability of fetal loss, consistent with observations from other species where living offspring can interfere in parental reproduction.
items.author: Nikolaos Smit, Berta Roura-Torres, Axelle Delaunay et al.

items.title: Folding without glutamine: Proteome-scale removal of a canonical amino acid
items.summary: by Alejandro Garciarrubio, Blanca Ramos-Cerrillo, Enrique Morett, Lorenzo Segovia All known life uses a canonical alphabet of 20 amino acids, yet which residues are structurally essential remains untested at proteome scale. Isoleucine was recently eliminated from ribosomal proteins in Escherichia coli , establishing that amino acid alphabet reduction is feasible. Here we ask whether an entire amino acid can be eliminated from a proteome, and develop a computational framework to identify the best target. Using two independent approaches — ProteinMPNN structure-based probabilities and multiple sequence alignment conservation — we define “keep-score” as the fraction of positions where the native residue is optimal.
items.author: Alejandro Garciarrubio, Blanca Ramos-Cerrillo, Enrique Morett et al.

items.title: The influence of ensemble size and composition on the performance of combined real-time COVID-19 forecasts
items.summary: by Friederike Becker, Katharine Sherratt, Nikos I. Bosse, Sebastian Funk During infectious disease outbreaks, short-term forecasts can play an important role for both decision makers and the general public. While previous research has shown that combining individual forecasts into an ensemble improves accuracy and consistency, practical guidance for organisers of multi-model prediction platforms on how to construct an ensemble has been scarce. In particular, it is not entirely clear how ensemble performance relates to the size of the underlying model pool, a relevant question when relying on voluntary contributions from modelling teams that face competing priorities. Furthermore, the exact composition of an ensemble forecast may influence its performance.
items.author: Friederike Becker, Katharine Sherratt, Nikos I. Bosse et al.

items.title: Global sensitivity analysis for stochastic models of infectious diseases: Re-emergence of yellow fever virus in the Americas as a case study
items.summary: by Nate Kornetzke, Helen J. Wearing Emerging infectious diseases are a persistent public health threat that challenge deterministic, mechanistic modeling approaches. Because outbreaks initially start with a low number of infected hosts, their dynamics are highly stochastic, making traditional deterministic methods, e.g., ordinary differential equations, unable to qualitatively or quantitatively capture the transmission dynamics. In place, stochastic models are used, such as Markov chain models, but these models present their own challenges. Often, to infer a quantity of interest with stochastic models, we need to sample the model’s distribution many times over, introducing an additional source of noise to our analysis.
items.author: Nate Kornetzke, Helen J. Wearing

items.title: Whole-proteome structure/function prediction in uropathogenic E. coli reveals previously missed host-microbe and microbe-phage interaction pathways
items.summary: by Chunxiang Peng, Henry Schreiber, Chengxin Zhang, Quancheng Liu, Scott Hultgren, Lydia Freddolino The rapid advancement of high-throughput sequencing technologies has vastly increased the number of known protein sequences, but the experimental characterization of their structures and functions lags behind. This gap in knowledge impedes our understanding of biological mechanisms of these proteins, hinders the interpretation of high-throughput experiments, and exposes a significant challenge in modern biology: deducing the structural and functional information of proteins based on their sequences. Most computational approaches rely on homology with well-annotated proteins, yet many proteins lack identifiable homologues, reducing the power of this approach.

items.title: A Plasmodium knowlesi A1-H.1 transcriptome time course focusing on the late asexual blood stages
items.summary: by Katlijn De Meulenaere, Dalia Díaz-Delgado, Pieter Monsieurs, Erin Sauve, Alfred Cortés, Ellen Knuepfer, Anna Rosanas-Urgell The zoonotic parasite Plasmodium knowlesi is closely related to Plasmodium vivax , the second leading cause of human malaria. P. knowlesi line A1-H.1 can be maintained in human erythrocytes and is an experimental model for P. vivax biology. We present the first transcriptome time course of the intraerythrocytic developmental cycle (IDC) of P. knowlesi A1-H.1 grown in human normocytes. Bulk RNA-sequencing was performed at five IDC stages using tightly synchronised cultures, enabling identification of constitutively expressed genes and stage-specific biomarkers, and investigation of temporal expression patterns of multigene families.

items.title: Acute Pancreatitis Caused by Impaction of Migrated Surgical Staples in the Duodenal Papilla After Distal Pancreatectomy.
items.summary: A 67-year-old woman underwent a laparoscopic distal pancreatectomy for pancreatic body cancer. On postoperative day (POD) 23, the patient presented with epigastric pain and was diagnosed with delayed peripancreatic fluid collection, which was treated with antibiotics and percutaneous drainage. On POD 51, the patient developed recurrent epigastric pain. Laboratory tests revealed elevated pancreatic enzyme and inflammatory marker levels. Computed tomography revealed acute pancreatitis and a high-density area in the duodenal papilla suggestive of a foreign body. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography revealed that the surgical staples were impacted in the minor duodenal papilla and were successfully removed. Although pancreatography did not demonstrate residual staples, three additional staples were subsequently removed from the pancreatic duct.
items.author: Inaba K, Motomura M, Azuma Y, Kimoto T, Takahashi H, Ueo T, Narita R, Tada K, Fukuzawa K, Mizukami K.

items.title: Type I IFN autoantibodies in three of seven Europeans with life-threatening Usutu virus infection.
items.summary: We previously reported that two of three patients with severe Usutu virus (USUV) disease carried circulating autoantibodies (auto-Abs) neutralizing type I IFNs (AAN-I-IFN). Here, we studied four additional patients, bringing the total number of European patients with life-threatening USUV infection to seven (Austria, n = 1; France, n = 1; Hungary, n = 4; Italy, n = 1). Three of these patients (all male, aged 43, 77, and 78 years, one French and two Hungarian) had blood auto-Abs neutralizing at least 10 ng/ml IFN-α2 and IFN-ω and at least 1 ng/ml IFN-β. They suffered from meningitis (n = 1), meningoencephalitis (n = 1), or myocarditis (n = 1).

items.title: PLP1 -Associated Demyelinating Neuropathy in 2 Female Patients.
items.summary: Objective The aim of this study was to report 2 unrelated women with demyelinating motor-predominant neuropathy in whom pathogenic variants in the proteolipid protein 1 gene ( PLP1 ) were identified. Methods Two unrelated female individuals underwent nerve conduction studies, EMG, evoked potential tests, neuroimaging, and targeted genetic testing. Results The first patient, a 34-year-old woman, presented with foot drop and had electroneurographic findings consistent with a demyelinating motor-predominant neuropathy, with genetic testing revealing a pathogenic PLP1 variant. The second patient, also middle-aged, had a different pathogenic PLP1 variant and a clinical diagnosis of progressive spastic paraplegia, with detailed electrophysiologic assessment demonstrating a coexistent demyelinating motor-predominant neuropathy.
